title: Court rules Pentagon can blacklist Anthropic for refusing to enable Claude features
gist: The DC Circuit ruled 2-1 that the Pentagon may designate Anthropic a supply-chain risk under 41 U.S.C. 4713 for withholding Claude features from the military, even without malicious intent, conflicting in effect with a Northern District of California ruling that found the parallel 10 U.S.C. 3252 designation unlawful; Anthropic is weighing en banc or Supreme Court review.

insights.claim: The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit ruled 2-1 that the Defense Department lawfully blacklisted Anthropic as a supply-chain risk for withholding certain Claude features from the military, even though Anthropic had no malicious intent.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: AI vendors that impose usage restrictions on government customers now face legal exposure to federal procurement bans, affecting government AI market share.
insights.locator: A US appeals court today approved

insights.claim: The Trump administration's March action ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic products and banned defense contractors from doing any business with Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The contractor ban extends the commercial impact beyond direct government sales to the whole defense-industrial base.

insights.claim: The two judges in the majority, Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao, were both Trump appointees who served in the first Trump administration; the dissent came from George H.W. Bush appointee Karen Henderson.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Panel composition raises odds of en banc rehearing being sought; outcome may hinge on court makeup.

insights.claim: A Northern District of California judge ruled the blacklisting illegal under 10 U.S.C. 3252, which limits supply-chain risk to adversaries acting maliciously, while the DC Circuit upheld it under the broader 41 U.S.C. 4713, over which Congress gave it exclusive jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The government has a statutory path (4713) to exclude domestic vendors without proving bad motive, a durable tool against any contractor that restricts product use.

insights.claim: The DC Circuit held that section 4713's use of 'any person' and the verb 'deny' covers a vendor preventing the government from using product features, so Anthropic disabling lawful Claude functions qualifies as a supply-chain risk.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Precedent that model-level safety restrictions can be treated as supply-chain risk pressures AI labs to offer unrestricted models to defense buyers.
insights.quote: we conclude that the Secretary’s concern about Anthropic disabling Claude from performing lawful actions requested by the Department qualifies as a ‘supply chain risk’ within the meaning of section 4713

insights.claim: Judge Henderson's dissent argued section 4713 targets deliberate impeding or eavesdropping by hostile actors and should not cover a contractor's honest, upfront enforcement of use restrictions the government dislikes.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The dissent provides a roadmap for en banc or Supreme Court review.

insights.claim: Judge Rita Lin in the Northern District of California found the blacklisting violated the First Amendment as retaliation after Anthropic refused to drop restrictions on lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance of Americans.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Conflicting rulings keep legal uncertainty high; the ultimate resolution may reach the Supreme Court.
insights.quote: The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics

insights.claim: The DC Circuit framed the case as a trade-off between overly constrained AI models shutting down and causing military operations to fail versus unconstrained models hallucinating inappropriate targets for lethal force, and left the balance to the President and Defense Secretary.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Courts are deferring to the executive on military AI policy, favoring vendors willing to accept fewer use restrictions.
insights.quote: overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and thus causing important military operations to fail

insights.claim: The court noted Claude's encoded restrictions had on more than one occasion stopped it from performing tasks requested by government users, and a dispute arose over whether contract terms barred Claude's use in an ongoing overseas military operation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Operational reliability under usage policies is now a procurement criterion for defense AI contracts.

insights.claim: Anthropic said it disagrees with the ruling and is considering all options including further review, via en banc rehearing or a Supreme Court petition.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Litigation overhang on Anthropic's government business likely persists for months.

insights.claim: Despite the litigation, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick recently said the Trump administration and Anthropic have patched up their relationship and are 'in tune'.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A political settlement could moot the legal fight; watch for any rescission of the designation.
